mill.summary: Argued that liberty should be limited only to prevent harm to others, and made an early philosophical case for the equality of women.

abolition-british.summary: The trade was outlawed in 1807 and slavery itself across most of the empire from 1834, with an intermediate period of compulsory unpaid "apprenticeship" that ended in 1838.
abolition-british.note: The 1833 Act compensated slave owners, not the enslaved; the resulting government debt was not finally repaid until 2015.

latin-american-independence.summary: Napoleon's occupation of Spain broke the link to the colonies, and within twenty-five years almost all of Spanish and Portuguese America was independent — Argentina in 1816, Chile 1818, Colombia 1819, Mexico and Peru 1821, Brazil 1822.

lincoln.summary: Held the United States together through the war that ended slavery in it, having entered office proposing only to stop slavery spreading, and was shot five days after the surrender.

dickens.summary: Published in monthly parts to enormous audiences, put the workhouse and the debtors' prison in front of readers who had not looked, and knew both from the inside at twelve.

boole.summary: Reduced logic to algebra, giving the true-and-false arithmetic that every digital circuit since has been built from — eighty years before there were any circuits to build.

lovelace.summary: Whose notes on the Analytical Engine include an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers, and the observation that such a machine might compose music — the first published sense of a computer as more than a calculator.
lovelace.note: Whether her notes constitute the first computer program is argued. What is not argued is that she saw the machine could operate on symbols rather than only numbers, which Babbage's own writing does not say.

zulu-kingdom.summary: Built by Shaka through military reorganisation, and remembered in Britain chiefly for destroying a British column at Isandlwana in 1879.

cholera-pandemics.summary: Seven pandemics since 1817, all originating in the Ganges delta. The 1854 London outbreak prompted John Snow to trace cases to a single water pump, which founded epidemiology and made the case for sanitation.

marx.summary: Analysed capitalism as a historical stage driven by class conflict, and insisted philosophy should change the world rather than interpret it.
marx.significance: Whatever one makes of the politics, the analytical move - treating economic arrangement as the thing that shapes belief rather than the reverse - is now assumed by historians of every persuasion.

dostoevsky.summary: Explored guilt, faith and freedom through fiction, staging the argument against God more forcefully than most believers dared.

greek-independence.summary: The first successful nationalist revolt against Ottoman rule, and the start of the empire's long unravelling in the Balkans.

mendel.summary: Worked out the statistical rules of inheritance by breeding pea plants, and was ignored for thirty-five years.

railways.summary: Land transport stopped being limited by how far a horse could walk in a day. Within seventy years railways had redrawn where people lived, made standard time necessary to run a timetable, and given empires a way to move troops and extract raw materials at speed.
railways.note: The bracket opens on the Stockton and Darlington and the Liverpool and Manchester, the first lines to carry the public behind steam, and closes once the world's main networks are built. Track kept being laid; the age of it being new did not.

tolstoy.summary: Turned from novels to a radical Christian ethic of nonviolence and voluntary poverty; his correspondence with Gandhi shaped satyagraha.

great-game.summary: Decades of manoeuvring between the Russian and British empires over Central Asia and Afghanistan, which drew borders still contested today.

trail-of-tears.summary: The forced march of the Cherokee, Choctaw, Muscogee, Chickasaw and Seminole west of the Mississippi, carried out after the Supreme Court had ruled against it, killing thousands on the way.

maxwell.summary: Unified electricity, magnetism and light into four equations, and predicted radio waves before anyone had made one.

mendeleev.summary: Arranged the elements by periodic properties and left gaps for ones not yet found, then saw them discovered where he said they would be.

telegraph.summary: The first time a message could outrun the person carrying it. News that had taken a ship three weeks to cross the Atlantic arrived in minutes, and markets, newspapers and governments reorganised themselves around it.
telegraph.note: The bracket closes at the first durable transatlantic cable. An 1858 cable worked for three weeks and failed, which is why 1866 rather than 1858 is the date that counts.

opium-wars.summary: Britain went to war twice to compel China to keep importing opium, winning treaty ports, extraterritoriality and Hong Kong. In China this opens what is still taught as the century of humiliation.

russian-conquest-central-asia.summary: Tsarist armies absorbed the khanates of Khiva, Bukhara and Kokand, closing the era of independent steppe states and bringing Russia to the borders of British India.

image.credit: Turkestan_1900-es.svg: Wassily / Translator:Molorco derivative work: HylgeriaK (talk)

monet.summary: Gave Impressionism its name with one canvas a critic mocked, then spent thirty years painting the same haystacks, cathedral and lily pond over and over to catch what the light did to them.

treaty-of-waitangi.summary: The founding document of New Zealand, signed in two versions that do not say the same thing — a discrepancy still being litigated.
treaty-of-waitangi.note: The Māori and English texts differ on the central point. The English cedes sovereignty; the Māori cedes kāwanatanga, or governorship, while retaining tino rangatiratanga, or full chieftainship.

image.credit: William Hobson, James Freeman, and James Busby (English version); Henry Williams and Edward Williams (Māori translation)

nietzsche.summary: Declared inherited moral certainties dead and asked what values a person might create once nothing is given.
nietzsche.significance: He asked what happens to morality when its foundations are no longer believed, which is why he is read as diagnosing the twentieth century he did not live to see.

new-zealand-wars.summary: Conflicts over land and sovereignty between the Crown and Māori iwi, followed by confiscations of territory from tribes deemed rebellious.

liberia-independence.summary: Founded by freed American slaves and declared independent in 1847, making it, with Ethiopia, one of only two African states to escape colonisation — at the cost of a settler elite ruling the indigenous majority.

taiping-rebellion.summary: A millenarian revolt led by a man who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus, which held much of southern China for over a decade.
taiping-rebellion.note: Death estimates range from 20 to 70 million, making it plausibly the deadliest civil war in history. The records are poor.

van-gogh.summary: Who painted for ten years, sold almost nothing, wrote his brother eight hundred letters explaining what he was trying to do, and became the template for how the public imagines an artist.

third-plague-pandemic.summary: Began in Yunnan and spread by steamship to every inhabited continent, killing over twelve million people, most of them in India. It was during this pandemic that the plague bacterium was finally identified.

tesla.summary: Whose alternating-current system won the argument about how to distribute electricity, and who died in a hotel room owed money by most of the industry he had made possible.

british-raj.summary: Direct Crown rule over the subcontinent following the rebellion of 1857 and the dissolution of the East India Company, ending with partition and independence.
british-raj.significance: India's share of world manufacturing fell from roughly a quarter to a few percent across the colonial period. The famines of these decades are counted in tens of millions.

image.credit: Edinburgh Geographical Institute; J. G. Bartholomew and Sons.

origin-of-species.summary: Set out evolution by natural selection with enough evidence to make it the organising principle of biology.
origin-of-species.significance: It supplied a mechanism, which is what earlier evolutionary ideas lacked. Everything in the Earth & Life lane above is legible because of it.

germ-theory.summary: Pasteur and Koch established that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, which made antisepsis and public sanitation rational.
germ-theory.significance: Accepting that specific organisms cause specific diseases is what made surgery survivable and public sanitation rational rather than merely tidy.
germ-theory.note: From Pasteur and Koch's work to general acceptance and the sanitation and antisepsis that followed from it.

impressionism.summary: Painters left the studio for daylight, helped by paint in tubes and by photography taking over the job of recording what things looked like — and were refused by the official Salon for their trouble.
impressionism.note: 1874 is the first independent exhibition, which gave the movement its name from a hostile review; 1886 is the eighth and last. The wider bracket allows for the work that led up to it.

residential-schools.summary: Indigenous children in Canada and the United States were removed to church- and state-run schools explicitly intended to erase their languages and cultures. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission described the policy as cultural genocide; unmarked graves are still being found.

tagore.summary: The first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, who wrote the words of two national anthems and spent his last decades arguing against the nationalism they were sung for.

us-civil-war.summary: Fought over whether slavery would expand, and settled by abolishing it, at a cost of roughly 750,000 lives.

blackbirding.summary: Around sixty thousand Pacific Islanders were taken, often by deception or force, to work sugar plantations in Queensland and Fiji — a coerced labour trade running decades after slavery was abolished elsewhere.

vivekananda.summary: Presented Vedanta to the West as a universal philosophy and pressed for a Hinduism expressed through service.

image.credit: The original uploader was Dziewa at English Wikipedia.

abolition-us.summary: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery after a civil war fought over it, though its exception for punishment of crime shaped incarceration for the next century and a half.

sun-yat-sen.summary: The figure both the Republic of China and the People's Republic still claim, whose movement ended two thousand years of imperial rule in 1911 and could not hold the country together afterwards.

marie-curie.summary: Discovered polonium and radium, coined the term radioactivity, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.
marie-curie.significance: Still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She died of the radiation she discovered, and her notebooks remain too radioactive to handle.

meiji-restoration.summary: Confronted with Western gunboats, Japan deliberately industrialised in a single generation — the only non-Western state to do so on its own terms in the nineteenth century.

gandhi-ahimsa.summary: Built a political method out of nonviolence and self-suffering, drawing on Jain ahimsa, the Gita and Tolstoy.
gandhi-ahimsa.significance: He turned a religious principle into a political method, and it was studied and reused from Selma to Soweto. Tolstoy's letters are part of its lineage.

lenin.summary: Argued that a disciplined party should seize power rather than wait for conditions to ripen, did it, and built a state whose founding assumptions outlived him by seven decades.

bertrand-russell.summary: Tried to ground mathematics in logic, helped found analytic philosophy, and was jailed twice for opposing war.

image.credit: Honourable Bertrand Russell.jpg: Photographer not identified derivative work: Conquistador

berdyaev.summary: Russian religious existentialist who put creative freedom at the centre of human dignity, and was expelled by the Soviet state for it.

churchill.summary: Prime minister through the years when Britain fought Germany alone, and an unreconstructed imperialist who expected to hold India afterwards and did not.
churchill.note: His record is genuinely double-sided — the wartime leadership is not in dispute, and neither is his imperialism, nor his government's conduct during the 1943 Bengal famine.

einstein.summary: Recast space and time as one flexible fabric shaped by mass, and showed light behaves as particles as well as waves.
einstein.significance: Relativity is not an adjustment to Newton but a replacement of what space and time are. GPS satellites must correct for it or drift kilometres off within a day.

image.credit: Photograph by Orren Jack Turner, Princeton, N.J. Modified with Photoshop by PM_Poon and later by Dantadd.

fleming-penicillin.summary: Noticed a mould killing bacteria on a contaminated plate, the observation that became penicillin and the antibiotic era.

picasso-cubism.summary: Broke the single viewpoint that European painting had used since the Renaissance, partly under the influence of African masks in a Paris museum, and spent seventy years refusing to settle into one manner.
picasso-cubism.note: The bracket is Picasso's life; Cubism itself is roughly 1907 to 1914, worked out with Georges Braque, who deserves half the credit and rarely gets it.

scramble-for-africa.summary: In roughly thirty years European powers moved from controlling coastal enclaves to occupying almost the entire continent. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

electrification.summary: Power that could be generated in one place and used in another ended the factory shaft that drove every machine from one engine, made the electric motor and the light bulb ordinary, and turned night into usable time.
electrification.note: The bracket opens at Edison's Pearl Street station, the first central generating plant selling power to the public, and closes when supply reaches most households in the industrialised world — decades later elsewhere, and still not everywhere.

emmy-noether.summary: Proved that every conservation law in physics follows from a symmetry, a result underpinning much of modern theory.

image.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Publisher: Mathematical Association of America [3], Brooklyn Museum [4], Agnes Scott College [5], [6]

berlin-conference.summary: European powers met to agree rules for claiming African territory. No African was present. The borders drawn there cut through peoples and polities and are, with few changes, the borders of today.
berlin-conference.significance: Borders drawn in a European room in two months still define African states today, which is why so many of them cut across peoples rather than between them.

bohr.summary: Modelled the atom with electrons confined to fixed energy levels and became the chief interpreter of quantum theory.

image.credit: The American Institute of Physics credits the photo [1] to AB Lagrelius & Westphal, which is the Swedish company used by the Nobel Foundation for most photos of its book series Les Prix Nobel.

congo-free-state.summary: Held as the personal property of Leopold II of Belgium and run for rubber through forced labour, mutilation and hostage-taking, until international revulsion forced its transfer to the Belgian state.
congo-free-state.note: Estimates of population decline run to around ten million, combining killing, starvation, disease and collapsed birth rates. No census exists for the period, so the figure is contested.

image.credit: See file history below for details.

ramanujan.summary: Produced thousands of identities in number theory with almost no formal training, some of which took a century to prove.
ramanujan.significance: He arrived at results that took a century to prove, largely self-taught from a single textbook. Some of his identities are still being found useful in unrelated fields.

schrodinger.summary: Wrote the wave equation describing how quantum states evolve, and posed the cat thought experiment to show how strange that was.

abolition-brazil.summary: The last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, and the destination of roughly four in ten of all Africans carried across the Atlantic.

cv-raman.summary: Found that light scattering off molecules shifts in wavelength, giving chemistry a way to fingerprint substances.

heidegger.summary: Reopened the question of what it means for anything to be, and made mortality and everyday absorption central to the answer.
heidegger.note: His membership of the Nazi party and refusal to renounce it remain central to how the work is assessed.

hubble.summary: Showed that the smudges in the telescope were other galaxies, and then that they are moving apart — which is how we know the universe has a history rather than just a size.

russian-flu-1889.summary: The first pandemic to spread along railways and telegraph-linked cities, killing around a million people and reported almost in real time.

wittgenstein.summary: Argued first that philosophy's problems dissolve once language is clear, then that meaning is use, refuting much of his own earlier work.

modernism.summary: A deliberate break with inherited form across painting, writing and music at once — cubism, atonality, stream of consciousness — driven by the sense that the old ways could not describe an industrial century, and hardened by the First World War.
modernism.note: One of the looser brackets here. Roots are commonly traced to Baudelaire and Manet in the 1860s; 1907 is Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, the usual marker for the break in painting; and the end is argued anywhere from 1930 to the 1960s. The bracket holds the period most accounts agree on and the note says what it leaves out.

wounded-knee.summary: US troops killed around three hundred Lakota, most of them unarmed and many women and children, in the event conventionally taken to close the Plains wars.

ambedkar.summary: Economist and jurist who dismantled the philosophical defence of caste, drafted India's constitution, and led a mass conversion to Buddhism.
ambedkar.significance: He dismantled the philosophical defence of caste, wrote the constitution of the country that practised it, and then left the religion that sanctioned it.

mao.summary: Won a civil war from the countryside, founded the People's Republic, and then launched the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which between them killed on a scale that has no agreed number.
mao.note: The death tolls of the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution are estimates and are contested; the lowest credible figures for the famine alone run to fifteen million and the highest to forty-five.

satyendra-bose.summary: Derived the statistics governing particles that can share a quantum state, the class since named bosons after him.

cinema.summary: A fairground novelty in 1895 that within a generation was the dominant narrative art of the century, and the first one whose works could be shipped and shown identically anywhere on earth.
cinema.note: The bracket runs from the Lumières' first paying audience to the arrival of synchronised sound, which is the point the form stopped being silent and became the one we recognise.

jazz.summary: Blues and ragtime met brass-band instruments in Black New Orleans and produced a music built on improvisation — which within fifty years had become the common language of popular music almost everywhere.
jazz.note: No single origin point survives scrutiny; the bracket opens on the New Orleans years from which the first recordings and first-hand accounts come. It stays open because the music did not stop.

krishnamurti.summary: Dissolved the organisation built to proclaim him a world teacher, then spent sixty years arguing that truth needs no authority at all.
